newsitem.title: USA: Clinton apologizes for black syphilis study.
newsitem.headline: Clinton apologizes for black syphilis study.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday apologized formally on behalf of the government to a group of black men whose syphilis went untreated for decades as part of a U.S. Public Health Service study.

"What was done cannot be undone but we can end the silence. We can stop turning our heads away. We can look at you in the eye and finally say on the behalf of the American people: What the United States did was shameful and I am sorry," Clinton told an emotional White House ceremony.

Five of the eight survivors of the health service study, which began in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1932 and lasted for 40 years, travelled to Washington for the ceremony. The others were too ill to participate.

"The American people are sorry for the loss, for the years of hurt. You did nothing wrong but you were grievously wronged. I apologise and I am sorry that this apology has been so long in coming," Clinton said. He said the government would help build a centre for bioethics and health care research in Tuskegee as part of a "lasting memorial."

The medical experiment involved 400 black men who were left untreated for syphilis for 40 years to allow doctors to study the course of the disease, even though antibiotic treatment was available. Survivors shared in a $10 million compensation award made by the government in 1974, but there has never been a formal apology until now.

Clinton told the survivors that those carrying out the experiment "diminished the stature of man by abandoning the most basic of precepts .... They had the power to heal the survivors and all the others and they did not. Today all we can do is apologise but you have the power ... only you have the power to forgive. Your presence here shows us that you have chosen a better path than your government did so long ago."
